author: Mark Atwood
text:
Resolved as documented contract, not a cap -- and the suggested fix would have introduced a worse bug than the one reported.

Why no cap. CertPool::add takes an already-decoded Certificate, so the allocation happened before the pool saw it: the pool holds what the caller already built rather than amplifying anything. CPU is bounded separately by PathBuilderConfig::dfs_budget, so a large pool makes path building slow, not unbounded. And the suggested 'generous like 1000' default would break legitimate use: CertPool is documented as the place to put ALL candidate intermediates, and a real intermediate cache (CCADB's set, for instance) runs to thousands. Any ceiling safe enough to matter is smaller than a legitimate pool somewhere.

The cited attack vector is already closed, as of PKIX-q9hv.33 earlier today. AIA-contributed certificates are bounded on every axis: max_response_bytes caps one response's bytes before parsing, max_certs_per_response caps certificates taken from one certs-only CMS bundle at 16, and max_total_fetches caps rounds at 8 -- so AIA can add at most 128 certificates to a pool. The 'CMS bag containing millions of certificates' cannot get past the byte cap.

Checked the other entry points: the only CertPool::from_iter call sites are pkix-difftest's PKITS and limbo corpus loaders, which read local fixture files, not untrusted input. pkix-chain's pool starts from supplied_chain, which is the caller's own data.

So the real obligation is at the step where untrusted bytes become certificates, which belongs to whoever parses them. That is now documented on CertPool, pointing at AiaConfig as the in-workspace worked example.

pkix-path-builder 0.5.2 for the doc change.
